item.title: U17WWC: You’ve written your names in gold – Tinubu tells Flamingos
item.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru President Bola Tinubu has congratulated Nigeria’s Flamingos for making history as the first African team to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup following their 2-1 victory over Japan in Saturday’s final in Rabat, Morocco. The president, who received the cheering news upon his return from campaign engagements in Akwa Ibom and Rivers States, hailed Nigeria’s maiden triumph as a proud moment for the nation and a landmark achievement for African women’s football. “What wonderful news to return home to! Our young girls have conquered the world and given Nigerians everywhere another reason to celebrate our great country. “To our gallant Flamingos, I say congratulations. You have shown courage, discipline, determination, and the Nigerian spirit of never giving up. “I followed your journey throughout this tournament, and after your semi-final victory, you promised to bring the trophy home. Today, you have kept that promise. You believed in yourselves, fought for one another, and carried our nation’s flag to the very top of the world. “Your victory is an inspiration to millions of young Nigerian girls who dream of achieving greatness. You have shown them that with hard work, opportunity, and determination, they too can reach the highest levels of achievement. “Today, Nigeria celebrates you. You have written your names in gold, and your country is immensely proud of you.” The president particularly applauds Awawu Bashiru and Oluebube Umejiaku, whose goals secured the historic victory, while commending the entire squad for their exceptional teamwork throughout the tournament. He also congratulates the coaching crew, the Nigeria Football Federation, and the National Sports Commission for their contributions to the team’s success. President Tinubu reaffirms his administration’s commitment to investing in grassroots sports development and expanding opportunities for young Nigerians, particularly girls, to discover, nurture, and fulfill their potential. “Congratulations once again, Flamingos. Thank you for making Nigeria proud.” The post U17WWC: You’ve written your names in gold – Tinubu tells Flamingos appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Rumbling in yoruba land: There’s only one Afenifere despite alleged breakup plan – Secretary
item.description: • Says Adebanjo endorsed Peter Obi in 2023 without telling anybody • Explains how Fasoranti endorsed Tinubu for president despite supplanting his leadership By Dapo Akinrefon Chief Ademola Folarin, a lawyer, is the General Secretary of the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere. Folarin, who is the Agbaakin Maiyegun of Ibadanland, in this interview, speaks on the leadership crisis in Afenifere, reconciliation in the group, and the decision of the Yoruba body to endorse President Bola Tinubu for 2027 among other issues. Excerpts: There have been issues in the polity ahead of 2027, parties have been trading accusations; there is mudslinging. Do you think this is healthy for our democracy? Look, adversarial politics is one of the hallmarks of democracy. You have to destroy one party in order for you to rise. It’s one of the pitfalls of democracy that we can’t avoid, which is why some people say democracy is not the best form of government. But we haven’t found a better one. I think we are just being dishonest. There is a better one, it’s not necessarily democratic. We can see it in China, we can see it in the Gulf states, a combination of constitutionalism and monarchy. In China, there is no monarchy, but they have a system of evolutionary leadership, and it is working. The trouble spots in the world are the democracies. Just look around you, everywhere you see a problem, it’s democratic. That’s because it has to be like that. If you want to see the downfall of someone to rise, you can’t have peace, you can’t have stability. The bastion of democracy, Europe and America, are on the decline. It’s consistent with the aims and objectives of the founding fathers of democracy. It was foreseen, but it was unavoidable. If you choose your leaders based purely on numbers, you cannot avoid obvious mistakes. In our country, with the presidential system, it is the same in America. We have simply imported a corrupt system here, presidential system. If you don’t have money, you can’t do anything. That’s what you have. Mudslinging, everything is part of it. Nigeria has practised the parliamentary system before. Now, it’s practising the presidential system. Which do you think Nigeria can adopt? Do you think it should jettison the two and have another system of government? It’s a no-brainer which one should prefer between the Westminster parliamentary system and the presidential system. item.title: ADC judgment could cause civil war if not properly managed—Amaechi
item.description: …Says mistake I made in 2023 was listening to Buhari By Olayinka Ajayi Vice presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, Mr Rotimi Amaechi, has warned that the Federal High Court judgment against the leadership of his party could trigger unrest. Last Thursday, the Federal High Court in Abuja nullified the National Working Committee led by former Senate President, David Mark, in a ruling that also invalidated the process that produced former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as the party’s presidential candidate for the 2027 elections. The judgment, delivered by Justice Peter Lifu, also nullified the emergence of former Minister of Interior, Rauf Aregbesola, as National Secretary, and other decisions taken by the Mark-led leadership, including the nomination of candidates for elective offices. The court further ordered the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, not to recognise or act on decisions taken at the party’s 99th National Executive Committee meeting of July 27, 2025. The judgment followed a suit, marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025, filed by former ADC Deputy National Chairman (North-East), Nafiu Gombe, who challenged the process through which Mark and other members of the caretaker committee assumed control of the party. Speaking in an interview on Mainland 98.3fm, Amaechi said: “It could cause a civil war if not properly managed. When we heard the news, we quickly met, myself and the presidential candidate and the chairman of the party, and we said: ‘please, lower the tempo’. I am not alleging, as there is a document signed by Nafiu resigning at the same time as Ralph Nwosu. There is a video of him behind David Mark handing over to David Mark. They go to hire, pay money, go to court and compromise some system here and there. There is no internal rift in our party, none. It is just the fear of the All Progressives Congress, APC. When they saw what happened in Sokoto, they began to cause a crisis that would frighten voters. Looking at things, which other party is opposing the APC other than ADC? The president is from the South-West, and we have three other presidential candidates in the South-West. Even if they don’t get every vote, they would certainly get some votes, and don’t forget the governor of Oyo State, Seyi Makinde, is also running. Let us assume he fails everywhere in the South-West; he will not fail in Oyo, where he comes from. Assuming he wins Oyo State, that is minus one for Tinubu. There is another presidential candidate from the South-East (Peter Obi) who will take away five states from the South-East. Already, he has lost six states from the South. The battle is in the South-South; I am their son. I am running as a vice presidential candidate. item.title: 68 days to polls: Struggling Nigerians make 2027 demands
item.description: • Send strong messages to Tinubu, Atiku, Obi, Makinde, Adebayo, Donald Duke, others • Affordability, security, steady power supply top list By Steve Oko, Olasukanmi Akoni, Esther Onyegbula, Cynthia Alo, Shina Abubakar, Rotimi Ojomoyela, Golok Nanmwa, James Ogunnaike, Musa Ubandawaki, Peter Duru, Haruna Aliyu, Deola Badru & Chiamaka Ekwuwe Hunger is biting harder, insecurity is spreading fear across communities, businesses are groaning under the weight of rising energy costs, and millions of Nigerians are struggling to survive on incomes that can hardly meet their basic needs. From the farmer afraid of returning to his farm to the unemployed graduate searching endlessly for a job, the average Nigerian is looking towards the 2027 general elections, with 68 days to the polls, with one overriding expectation: a president who will make life worth living again. With the political atmosphere charged ahead of the presidential election, Nigerians across the country have sent a strong message to the presidential candidates: the next occupant of Aso Rock must move beyond campaign rhetoric and confront hunger, poverty, insecurity, unemployment, inflation and the worsening living conditions of citizens. Expectations The expectations are particularly high as President Bola Ahmed Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress (APC) seeks another mandate, facing an array of contenders, including former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress (ADC); former Anambra State Governor, Peter Obi, of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC); Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde, of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM); Senator Sandy Ojang Onor of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP); former Cross River State Governor, Donald Duke, of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP); Omoyele Sowore of the African Action Congress (AAC); and Adewole Adebayo of the Social Democratic Party (SDP). Other candidates on the Independent National Electoral Commission’s published list include Sunday Chibuzo Okereke of the Labour Party (LP), Rufai Adekunle Omo-Aje of the Action Alliance (AA), Abbas-Bin Aliyu of the Action Democratic Party (ADP), Yusuf Kabiru of the Allied Peoples Party (APP), Sunday Adenuga of the Boot Party (BP), Moses Olusoji Adebisi of the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA), Ada Elizabeth Frederick Okwori of the National Democratic Party (NDP), Nkem Esther Okereke of the National Rescue Movement (NRM), Peter Ada Agada of the Young Progressives Party (YPP) and Daniel Daberechukwu Nwanyanwu of the Zenith Labour Party (ZLP). Survival Beyond the political parties, personalities and permutations surrounding the election, those who spoke to Sunday Vanguard in this public opinion survey said their concerns are fundamentally about survival, dignity and a better future. item.title: 2027: Ask Atiku where he got money to build university
item.description: •Shettima hits Obi •Yari targets 2.3m votes in Rivers •President will get 3m votes — Fubara By Henry Umoru, Omeiza Ajayi and Daniel Abia President Bola Tinubu yesterday challenged Nigerians to ask former Vice President Atiku Abubakar how he acquired the money to establish his university while serving in government, accusing him of using public resources to advance private interests. Tinubu, who spoke at the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally, held at the Adokiye Amiesimaka Stadium, Port Harcourt, Rivers State, also thanked Governor Siminalayi Fubara for his handling of the political crisis in the state, assuring him that he would not regret supporting him (Tinubu). The President, who is seeking a second term in the January 16, 2027 presidential election, urged Rivers residents to renew the mandate they gave him and Vice President Kashim Shettima in 2023. He also praised the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, for his development efforts and political support, describing him as a dependable partner in his administration. Taking a swipe at opposition politicians who have criticised his government’s handling of the economy, particularly the rising cost of living and hardship, Tinubu said those accusing his administration of creating hunger were responsible for the problems they now complain about. “Those people, talking of hunger, are clearly the mess they created. Atiku was one of them,” he said.\ “Ask him how he built the university, while he was in office as vice president in charge of our economy. Who built the university for you? It’s your money. It’s your effort. A man without moral integrity, rectitude and ethics for the office,” Tinubu said. The President’s remarks came amid renewed political exchanges between the ruling party and opposition figures ahead of the 2027 general election. Tinubu also used the occasion to express appreciation to Fubara for maintaining peace in Rivers State following the political confrontation that had threatened the stability of the state government. “I want to thank you specifically, for your maturity, understanding, respect for the wisdom of elders. When we intervened, you respected our position. You maintained peace. You are a committed democrat. Fubara, you will not regret what you have done,” he said. Recalling the support Rivers State gave him during the 2023 presidential election, Tinubu said the people stood by him at a time when his political fortunes appeared uncertain. “Rivers State, you have been good to me. In 2023, when I looked very helpless, you stood out to support me. Today again, I return here to say thank you. And seek your support for the second term,” he said. item.title: Institutional Memory, Professional Knowledge and the CORFEPS Journal
item.description: By Tunji Olaopa The Council of Retired Federal Permanent Secretaries (CORFEPS) is an association of patriotic former public servants that embodies administrative experiences, institutional memories and professional knowledge that could pull a lot of political and administrative weight within the reform imperative to transform governance architecture, the civil service and its ecosystem. As a multidisciplinary body of retired public servants with vast knowledge of the workings of the system, CORFEPS possesses a huge significance in connecting the institutional and reform dots in terms of where the civil service system is coming from, where it is at the moment and where it intends to be, given the democratic imperatives and development necessities of the current Tinubu administration. It is one of the most critical stakeholders in the public administration communities of practice and service that articulates a continuing professional and institutional interest in furthering the relevance of the civil service as a significant player in the development process in Nigeria. The necessity of such a body derives from the fact that patriotic and meritorious service does not need to end with retirement. Indeed, more can still be done in entrenching the institutional memories that retired permanent secretaries embody. CORFEPS, under the able chairmanship of Mahmud Yayale Ahmed, has been energetic in its consistent push to regain the vocational honor, professional ethos and administrative efficiency of the civil service. And in furtherance of this enthusiastic push for the significance of the civil service system as one critical cornerstone of democratic governance in Nigeria, CORFEPS has just launched an amazing initiative: the CORFEPS Journal on Pubic Policy and Governance. This significant initiative must be situated within a larger context of the institutional reform of the civil service system, especially its status as a value-based institution founded on merit, public spiritedness and professionalism. That context facilitates a framework that allows the past and the present to initiate conversation, and for both retired and current public servants to incessantly brainstorm the future of the bureaucratic system and its capability readiness to shoulder the burden of public policy implementation. The journal, I must say, presses the advantage of escalating the fundamental significance of professional knowledge and its role in deepening institutional progress. In other words, through it, CORFEPS provides a rare forum—draw, I dare say, from the administrative history of that golden era when administrative theorists (the gown) and practitioners (the town) were in conversation—within which administrative ideas, practices and initiatives could be discussed, extended and applied. item.title: AMERICA IS NOT NIGERIA: Why Trump’s midterm defeat cannot predict Tinubu’s 2027 fortunes
item.description: By Kayode Akinmade The sweeping defeat suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 American midterm elections has predictably provided fresh ammunition for Nigeria’s opposition politicians, who are already attempting to draw parallels between the political fortunes of the American president and those of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections. While the comparison may offer an attractive political talking point, it is, at best, superficial and, at worst, a deliberate attempt to transplant the political circumstances of one country into another. There is no doubt that the Republican defeat represents a significant setback for Trump. Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a powerful electoral rebuke to the Republican administration and signalling widespread dissatisfaction with some of its policies. The result has opened a new chapter in American politics and raised questions about the direction of Trump’s presidency. However, the critical question is whether the circumstances that produced this outcome in the United States are sufficiently comparable to Nigeria’s political and economic realities to justify the conclusion that Tinubu is destined for a similar electoral fate in 2027. The answer is no. America is not Nigeria. Trump is not Tinubu. And the political dynamics of the United States cannot be mechanically imported into Nigeria’s electoral calculations. Indeed, one of the most important factors behind the Republican Party’s defeat was the controversial war involving the United States and Iran, a foreign policy decision that has generated enormous economic, diplomatic and security consequences for the Trump administration. The conflict, which has lasted several months, has heightened concerns about American military involvement abroad, increased pressure on energy markets and contributed to rising fuel prices. For American households already grappling with the cost of living, the war became another source of economic anxiety. Its financial implications, military casualties and uncertain strategic objectives also generated questions about the wisdom of the administration’s foreign policy choices. Iran conflict Significantly, the political consequences were acknowledged by the highest levels of the American government. Trump admitted that the Iran conflict contributed to his party’s electoral difficulties, although he maintained that the military action was necessary. His Vice President, JD Vance, was considerably more direct, declaring that “the reason we lost is the war.” That admission is particularly instructive. It establishes that the Republican defeat was not simply an abstract expression of public dissatisfaction with a sitting president. It was substantially connected to identifiable policy decisions and their consequences for American voters. item.title: Countdown to 2027: Edo North is for Oshiomhole
item.description: By Allison Abanum Adams Oshiomhole’s first term has been defined by a deliberate strategy of translating legislative power into tangible federal presence for Edo North. As Chairman of the Senate Committee on Interior, he has leveraged his position to facilitate federal employment for constituents and ensure fair representation in federal institutions. His legislative record includes moving over 10 motions and sponsoring many bills. These are not abstract motions; they are institutional investments that will outlast any single political cycle. On the ground, Oshiomhole constituency interventions have reached all wards in Edo North, a coverage rate that speaks to both reach and intentionality. Oshiomhole has moved from delivering roads to delivering accountability, and Edo North have seen the difference in both bricks and budgets. Beyond infrastructure, his engagement with youth leaders and traditional rulers signals a recognition that representation must be relational, not transactional, a point underscored by his refusal to charge constituents for assistance and his warning against extortion in his name. The political consolidation around Oshiomhole 2027 bid reflects a broader strategic calculation within Edo North. Endorsements have since crossed traditional lines: From the market women in Auchi to the Artisan in Iyahmo, down to all the student bodies and community leaders, it is clear that it is no longer a question of whether Edo North is standing for Oshiomhole; it is a question of how loudly Edo North will say so. To the people in the rural areas of Edo North, they have risen from service, unity, and discipline: delivery that touches households, reconciliation that silences internal friction, and grassroots organisation that turns intention into votes. The good people of Edo North on their own are moving ward by ward to get support for Oshiomhole. The plough is heavy; the hands must be steady because the furrow ahead is 2027. The message is clear: no retreat, no sideways glance, no nostalgia for old battles in Edo North. A senatorial district that has seen the light and future must now prove it can cultivate it, row by row, ward by ward, state by state, until the harvest of triumph is achieved. Every leader, every member, every supporter keeps eyes on the furrow, not on the noise. So, let the word go forth: APC is on the plough, and there is no looking back until Oshiomhole is sent back to the Senate in 2027. The task is not to boast of yesterday but to labour for tomorrow with humility, focus, and determination. The harvest belongs to those who keep ploughing. For a senatorial district that has historically oscillated between alignment and agitation, the emerging consensus is that Oshiomhole federal network is an asset too valuable to surrender. Abanum lives in Abuja. The post Countdown to 2027: Edo North is for Oshiomhole appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: A Ballot on a Burial Date? Northern Nigeria Confronts the Symbolism of January 16
item.description: By Hassan A Karofi The choice of dates in politics is often presented as a matter of administrative convenience. Yet history teaches us that dates carry powerful symbolism, especially in societies where collective memories of tragedy and triumph remain deeply rooted. As Nigeria prepares for a presidential election scheduled for January 16, 2026, it is important to reflect on what that date means to millions of people, particularly in Northern Nigeria, where January 16 is associated with one of the darkest episodes in the country’s history. The significance of January 16 cannot be understood without revisiting the events of the country’s first military coup. In the early hours of January 15, 1966, a group of young military officers launched Nigeria’s first coup d’état. By the morning of January 16, the consequences of the coup were evident. Several of Nigeria’s most prominent political and military leaders had been assassinated. Among those killed were Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto and Premier of Northern Nigeria; Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, Nigeria’s first Prime Minister; Brigadier Samuel Ademulegun; Brigadier Zakariya Maimalari; and other senior political and military figures. While leaders from different regions were affected, the perception in the North was that the coup disproportionately targeted Northern political leadership. This perception would profoundly shape political attitudes and inter-ethnic relations for decades. The events following the coup further deepened Northern grievances. Major General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi assumed power and suspended parts of the constitutional order. In many parts of Northern Nigeria, suspicion and anger grew rapidly, culminating in the counter-coup of July 1966. The resulting instability ultimately contributed to the chain of events that led to the Nigerian Civil War. More than six decades later, the memory of January 1966 remains alive. For many Northern families, historians, traditional institutions, and political observers, January 16 is not merely another date on the calendar. It is a reminder of a traumatic turning point that altered Nigeria’s political trajectory and claimed the lives of leaders who continue to be revered across the region. Against this backdrop, the decision to hold a presidential election on January 16 raises legitimate questions. Whether the date was chosen for logistical, constitutional, or electoral reasons, policymakers should recognize that symbolism matters in politics. Elections are national events meant to unite citizens around a shared democratic purpose. When an election coincides with a date associated with historical mourning for a significant section of the country, there is a risk that the symbolism overshadows the democratic exercise itself. This concern is not necessarily about rejecting the election or questioning its legitimacy. Rather, it is about understanding how political decisions are perceived. item.title: 2027: Between Okowa and Ochei, a Trojan horse race?
item.description: By Emmanuel l. Nwagboniwe Let’s not equivocate here. The indices and optics in the political space amply suggest that the electoral race to represent Delta North in the Senate in 2027 is a direct contest between the former Delta State Governor, Dr. Ifeanyi Okowa of the All Progressives Congress (APC ), and ex -Speaker of the Delta State House of Assembly, Victor Ochei of the National Democratic Party (NDC). Evidently, the projection of a contest likely to throw up soap- box rhetoric, anxieties, euphoria, and political high drama, horse trading, and possibly, mudslinging, is a no-brainer: Okowa and Ochei have bounced into the political ring with unequalled superlatives and robust social capital. Commendably too, these former political allies’ ‘roll call of honour’ tells a convincing story of remarkably impressive private and public service careers- years put in and sacrificed largely in selfless and people-centred engagements. For instance, a studied glance at Dr Ifeanyi Okowa’s resume speaks volumes: medical doctor; council chairman; Commissioner of Health; Secretary to the Delta State Government (SSG); Senator of the Federal Republic of Nigeria; two- term Governor of Delta State, ex -Vice Presidential candidate of the People’s Democratic Party (PDP) in the 2023 General Election. Conversely, Victor Ochei is equally a no fresher in the public cum political space. He is a graduate of Chemical Engineering; Founder/ Chairman of Day Notch Nigeria Limited, an engineering firm of global status; Member, Delta State House of Assembly representing Aniocha North Council; Deputy Minority Leader; Speaker, Delta State House of Assembly; Executive Director, Maritime Labour and Cabotage Services at the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency (NlMASA); President, Nigerian Tennis Federation, among others. Without gas lighting, these political highflyers’ ‘selling points’ make any of them eminently qualified to represent the Anioma nationality in the Red Chamber. However, one knows that making a choice out of these two top contenders, especially by voters in a dynamic and highly unpredictable democratic space like ours where selfish and primordial sentiments hold sway, is certainly a herculean task, yet a candidate’s ‘report card’ remains an added advantage. For Okowa, he is majorly regarded as a grassroots politician who walks his talk in terms of mass mobilisation, especially across the nine councils that make up the Delta North Senatorial District. Evidently too, the former governor’s enduring stay in the political trenches for over three decades tells a reassuring story of one who understands the undercurrents and dynamics of power ‘capture’. Moreover, Okowa has other political assets to take to the electioneering field; he has a vast and extensive experience in the executive and the legislative arms of government, and no matter how hard his traducers knock him, he being an ex -state executive, has a chunk of tangible and verifiable score cards to pr

item.title: FG plans National Sports Commission office in Kwara – Magaji
item.description: By Demola Akinyemi ILORIN – The Federal Government has concluded plans to establish an office of the National Sports Commission (NSC) in Kwara State, following the development of sports facilities by the administration of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq. The Executive Chairman of the Kwara State Sports Commission, Coach Bola Magaji, disclosed this in Ilorin, saying officials of the NSC had been impressed by the facilities provided by the state government. Magaji spoke at the unveiling of a book titled The Sardauna of Ilorin in the Eyes of History, written in honour of AbdulRazaq, who holds the traditional title of Sardauna of Ilorin. The book was authored by Abiodun Abdul Kareem, a senior journalist and editor of Herald on Sunday, the Sunday publication of the Kwara State Printing and Publishing Corporation. Magaji recalled that officials of the National Sports Commission visited Kwara about three weeks ago to assess the sports facilities developed by the AbdulRazaq administration over the past seven years. He said the officials expressed satisfaction with the facilities at the state stadium complex and indicated that the proposed NSC office would be established in the state. According to him, the development reflects the growing recognition of Kwara’s investment in sports infrastructure. Magaji said the state’s stadium complex could boast of some of the best squash court facilities in the world, adding that Kwara contingents to national and international sporting competitions had recorded improved medal-winning performances. He attributed the development to investments in sports infrastructure and efforts to promote sporting activities in the state. Also speaking, the Special Adviser and Counsellor to the Governor, Alhaji Saad Salahudeen, said AbdulRazaq’s contributions to governance, politics, youth development and national development would continue to attract attention in the years ahead. He said the governor’s footprints in public service would remain relevant and be referenced in the next 50 years. Earlier, the Chairman of the Organising Committee, Mallam Umar Abdulwahab, said the event was designed to provide a platform for discussions on leadership, public service, governance and historical preservation. He said the initiative was also aimed at documenting experiences and inspiring future generations. The event was attended by several dignitaries, including the Emir of Ilorin, Alhaji Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, who was represented by Magaji Ogundele; Alhaji Saad Kajola; Alhaji Yusuf Abdullahi; the Secretary to the State Government, Professor Mamman Jibril; Senior Adviser on Islamic Religion, Alhaji Ibrahim Danmegoro; and Senior Adviser on Political Communication, Alhaji Bashir Adigun, among others. The post FG plans National Sports Commission office in Kwara – Magaji appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: A DECADE OF ROYAL SPLENDOUR: Oba Ewuare II’s 10th coronation anniversary
item.description: By Moses Stowe There are moments in the history of a people when the past and the present meet in a compelling celebration of identity, pride and continuity. For the people of the ancient Benin Kingdom, the 10th Coronation Anniversary of His Royal Majesty, Omo N’Oba N’Edo Uku Akpolokpolo, Ewuare II, CFR, the Oba of Benin, represents one such moment. A decade after ascending the revered throne, the monarch’s anniversary provides an opportunity to celebrate the enduring institution of the Benin monarchy, reflect on its contributions to cultural preservation and reaffirm the values that have sustained the kingdom across generations. More than a ceremonial commemoration, the anniversary brings together culture, history, sports, intellectual discourse, community engagement and royal pageantry in a programme designed to showcase the richness of Benin heritage. For Eagle Aromatic Schnapps, Nigeria’s Authentic Traditional Prayer Drink, culture is more than a reflection of the past; it is a living heritage that connects generations, reinforces communal identity and preserves the values that define a people. This belief finds meaningful expression in the 10th Coronation Anniversary of His Royal Majesty, Oba Ewuare II, CFR, the Oba of Benin Kingdom. As a brand whose identity is rooted in Nigeria’s traditional heritage, Eagle Aromatic Schnapps recognises the significance of royal institutions as custodians of history, customs and cultural continuity. Its association with this historic milestone reflects the brand’s appreciation of the traditions that have sustained the Benin Kingdom and contributed to Nigeria’s diverse cultural identity. Eagle Aromatic Schnapps identifying with the anniversary goes beyond participating in a royal celebration. It represents an opportunity to reaffirm the importance of cultural preservation, community engagement and respect for the traditional institutions that continue to shape the country’s social fabric. Speaking on the significance of the anniversary, John Bamgbose, Assistant Brand Manager, Schnapps and Gin, Intercontinental Distillers Limited, described the occasion as an opportunity to celebrate the Benin Kingdom’s rich history and the values that connect generations. item.title: 2027: Danladi vows to build on AbdulRazaq’s achievements
item.description: By Demola Akinyemi ILORIN – The governorship candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Kwara State, Rt. Hon. Salihu-Yakubu Danladi, has said his seven years of experience in the legislature and familiarity with the state’s development challenges have prepared him to govern the state. Danladi, who is also the Speaker of the Kwara State House of Assembly, pledged to consolidate the achievements of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq and take the state to greater heights if elected in the 2027 governorship election. He said Kwara needed continuity and further development rather than a return to what he described as its ugly past. The APC candidate spoke during the News Keg, an interactive programme organised by the Kwara State Correspondents’ Chapel of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), where he discussed his political journey, legislative experience, achievements and development agenda ahead of the 2027 election. Danladi maintained that he was not a political novice, having served as Speaker since 2019 and participated in legislative processes supporting the present administration’s programmes. “I am not new to what is happening in Kwara State today. I have spent seven years in the legislature. No other candidate had any experience in government. I know virtually every sector and the challenges confronting the state,” he said. He argued that his legislative experience had given him a broad understanding of governance, particularly through the House of Assembly’s appropriation and oversight responsibilities, which he said complemented the executive’s implementation of policies and projects. The governorship candidate, an electrical engineering graduate, also highlighted his academic pursuits, disclosing that he had undertaken programmes in revenue management, peace, conflict and security studies and was currently pursuing a PhD in economic development. Reflecting on his representation of Ilesha/Gwanara Constituency, Danladi identified access to potable water, rural roads, healthcare, education and security as some of the major challenges that informed his legislative interventions. He said he facilitated the provision of about 210 boreholes across communities in his constituency during his first term, alongside the construction and rehabilitation of rural roads. One of the projects he highlighted was a 33-kilometre road linking communities in the constituency, which he said had significantly improved movement in the area. According to him, residents previously endured several hours of travelling during the rainy season for journeys that would ordinarily take about 30 minutes. item.title: Receive what you confess, by Funmi Komolafe
item.description: Gradually, year 2026 is drawing to an end. Being alive is a reason we must continuously thank God. Brethren, have you said thank you Jesus this morning? Please do. You owe the Lord gratitude. Beloved, last week we mentioned confession as a key to a miracle. Today, we’ll return to that with more details. I’ll start with an uncommon story of the son of a farmer whose father was regarded as poor in a town. This young boy went to the farm with his father and he saw man drive past them in an exotic car. The boy looked back admired the car and said to himself “ I am going to drive a better car in this town”. That was decades ago, today that boy now a man is perhaps the richest person in that town of course with the best cars in that town but he took some steps. We’ll return to in the article. Brethren, let’s go to the spiritual. The word of the Lord tells us in Proverbs 18 vs. 21 ( NIV) “ the tongue has the power of life and death, and those who love it eat its fruit”. The son of a farmer used his tongue positively and he is eating the fruits of the words that he spoke to himself today. As Christians however, we need not use the tongue casually as the farmer’s son did. We need to use the tongue in line with the word of God. How then do we use the appropriate word? The answer is found in the word of Prophet Joshua in Joshua 1 vs.8: “ Do not let this Book of the Law depart from your mouth; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do every written in it. Then you will be prosperous and successful”. The importance of tongue that God has given to all human beings is repeated in Psalm 1 vs. 2: “ But his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night”. Just as you need to study to pass an exam you need to study the Word of God to be able to confess it. Confession in this case is not about the sins you have committed but it’s about saying what God has promised you and your desire to have it. To confess it, you need to memorize that particular verse of the Bible and say it to yourself. In other words, you need to put the words you have memorized into action by saying it to yourself and as you do so, if no human being sees you, the invisible God is watching and listening to you. How do I know? I knew a woman that was barren for over 20 years. She learnt the word by going to church regularly and reading the Holy Bible on her own. It was during one of those church services that she picked up two verses. The first, is Deuteronomy 7 vs. 14: “ You will be blessed more than any other people, none of your men or women will be childless, nor any of your livestock without young”. The second is Exodus 23 vs.26: “ and none shall miscarry or be barren in your land. I will give you a full life span”.
